source_user: Explain how KV cache changes between training and inference. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: In autoregressive inference, each layer stores the key and value tensors for tokens already processed and appends the new token's K/V at every decode step. Attention can then read the stored prefix instead of recomputing its projections, reducing repeated work but consuming memory roughly in proportion to layers, active tokens, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per element. Standard teacher-forced training normally processes a whole batch sequence in a forward/backward graph and retains or recomputes activations for gradients rather than maintaining a persistent per-request serving cache. Boundary condition: packed, chunked, or specialized training implementations can change activation and attention memory, so the exact implementation must be measured rather than inferred from serving cache capacity.
risks: Training activation memory and inference cache memory have different lifetimes and should not be conflated.
evidence_required: Record the training attention implementation, sequence packing, precision, and separate inference cache occupancy.

source_user: Explain how KV cache changes between training and inference. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Inference uses an incremental per-sequence KV cache: after the prompt is processed, prior K/V tensors remain resident and only the newest token's K/V is appended, avoiding a full-prefix recomputation at each step. Ordinary full-sequence training uses teacher forcing and computes gradients for the batch, so its memory is dominated by weights, optimizer state, activations, and implementation-specific attention work rather than a persistent serving cache. Boundary condition: gradient checkpointing, flash-attention variants, and sequence packing can substantially change training memory, while inference memory scales with active tokens and concurrency; compare measured budgets only under stated configurations.
risks: A statement about training memory is incomplete without specifying forward/backward mode, precision, and attention implementation.
evidence_required: Report peak training memory and inference cache bytes separately with model and runtime settings.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about KV cache and correct it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: KV cache is free memory that always makes generation faster. Correction: it trades memory for less repeated prefix work. During decode, stored per-layer K/V tensors are reused while the new token is appended, but the cache grows with active sequence tokens and can reduce the room available for batching. Boundary condition: once HBM pressure causes paging, offload, eviction, smaller batches, or admission rejection, the memory traffic and scheduling effects can erase or reverse the latency or throughput benefit.
risks: The observed benefit depends on workload shape and serving policy, not only on the cache algorithm.
evidence_required: Measure HBM peak, cache occupancy, paging/offload events, batch size, and latency percentiles.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about KV cache and correct it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: caching makes every token's attention constant-cost. Correction: it removes recomputation of earlier K/V projections, but each new query still attends over the growing prefix, and the stored K/V must be read. The cache therefore saves one class of repeated work while adding memory traffic and capacity demand. Boundary condition: for short prompts or memory-bandwidth-bound kernels, cache reads and launch/scheduling overhead may dominate, so a speedup should not be assumed.
risks: Exact attention complexity and bottleneck depend on architecture, kernel, sequence length, and hardware.
evidence_required: Use profiler counters and matched latency measurements across prompt lengths; do not infer cost from a single run.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about KV cache and correct it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: the cache size is determined only by the model's maximum context window. Correction: live cache allocation is also determined by the number of active sequences, their actual token lengths, layer count, KV-head layout, head dimension, precision, block metadata, and allocator overhead. Its mechanism is reuse of prior K/V tensors instead of recomputing them at later decode steps. Boundary condition: a context limit is a per-sequence validity constraint, whereas total HBM capacity can be exhausted earlier by concurrent requests and resident weights or workspace.
risks: A theoretical byte formula may omit fragmentation, metadata, padding, and other resident allocations.
evidence_required: Record actual cache allocation and HBM peak over a concurrency and length sweep.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about KV cache and correct it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: enabling a KV cache guarantees lower end-to-end latency. Correction: it reuses each layer's stored K/V for prior tokens, avoiding repeated prefix processing during incremental decoding; this can improve decode efficiency but does not eliminate prompt-processing time or queueing. Boundary condition: if cache memory lowers feasible concurrency or triggers eviction, paging, or request rejection, total p95/p99 latency may worsen even when isolated token computation is cheaper.
risks: TTFT, TPOT, queueing delay, and end-to-end latency can move differently.
evidence_required: Report TTFT, TPOT, queueing time, end-to-end percentiles, cache events, and admission outcomes separately.

source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: more cache capacity always increases throughput. Correction: the cache stores prior K/V tensors so decode steps reuse prefix projections, but allocating more of finite HBM to cache can displace workspace or reduce the space available for useful batching. Boundary condition: when the workload has little prefix reuse or is already compute-bound elsewhere, extra cache capacity may have no measurable benefit and can add management overhead.
risks: Throughput comparisons are confounded if cache capacity changes batch limits or other memory reservations.
evidence_required: Hold model, kernels, scheduler, and workload constant while sweeping cache capacity; record throughput, batch size, HBM, and cache hit/reuse behavior.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for KV cache. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Hypothesis: retaining prior K/V tensors reduces repeated prefix work and improves decode latency or tokens/s. Run the same fixed request trace on the same model, precision, hardware, engine, scheduler, prompt/output-length distribution, and concurrency with cache enabled and with a supported recomputation reference; warm up, randomize run order, and repeat each condition. Measure TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, HBM peak, cache occupancy, batch size, OOMs, and rejections. Boundary condition: if the reference changes batching or kernels, label the comparison non-equivalent and interpret it cautiously.
risks: A no-cache reference may not exist or may measure a different execution path.
evidence_required: Preserve raw per-request metrics, run order, seeds if applicable, and exact configuration for both conditions.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for KV cache. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Use a small factorial sweep over prompt length, generated length, and concurrency. For every cell, replay identical requests against cache-enabled serving and a valid recomputation baseline, keeping model revision, precision, GPU, engine, scheduler, arrival pattern, and batch policy fixed; warm up and repeat enough times to estimate variance. The mechanism under test is reuse of stored K/V tensors during later decode steps. Measure TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end percentiles, throughput, HBM peak, cache bytes, batch size, and failures. Boundary condition: stop or separately report cells that hit OOM, eviction, paging, or admission limits rather than treating them as ordinary latency samples.
risks: Averages can hide tail latency and failures at high concurrency.
evidence_required: Publish per-cell sample counts, confidence/variance summaries, raw failures, and cache event logs.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for KV cache. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Define a fixed model and request corpus, then compare cache-on execution with a supported cache-off or recomputation reference. Sweep at least two prompt lengths and two concurrency levels, keep output limits and arrival schedule fixed, warm up both treatments, and repeat each cell. Record TTFT and TPOT separately, end-to-end p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, GPU utilization, HBM peak, cache occupancy, batch size, OOMs, and rejections. Mechanism: stored K/V avoids recomputing prior-token projections during incremental decoding. Boundary condition: cache pressure can trigger eviction or offload and change the execution regime, so those events must be analyzed as outcomes rather than silently pooled.
risks: Changing the baseline's scheduler or batching behavior can confound the cache effect.
evidence_required: Archive exact runtime settings and raw per-request timings for every experimental cell.
